titleStmt.title: How good are my data and what is the resolution?
titleStmt.author: Philip R. Evans
Garib N. Murshudov

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: How good are my data and what is the resolution?

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: WHERE TO CUT A DATA SET OFF - the resolution limit every crystal structure declares, tested against refinement, automated model building and simulated data, and then explicitly refused as a rule
span.quote: A major cause of user indecision and conflicts with journal referees is the resolution cutoff. We cannot set definite rules for this, as it depends on what the data are to be used for. It is therefore a mistake to prematurely apply a harsh cutoff at the data-reduction stage: data can always be excluded later. It is also unclear how best to handle anisotropy: do you choose the best direction or the worst? It is probably best to include data to the limit in the best direction.

span.label: at what point weak high-resolution data stop carrying information, and whether any of the data-processing statistics marks that point
span.quote: How can we decide where to apply a resolution cutoff? On the one hand, using high-resolution data which are so weak as to be insignificant will add nothing useful, may add unwanted noise to maps and may lead us to overconfidence in the quality of our model (although the relationship between data quality and model quality is not clear). On the other hand, we do not want to exclude useful data which might aid structure solution and improve the final model. Anisotropy in the data complicates this decision, as it is not clear whether it is better to include data based on the best direction, the worst, or something in between. Anisotropic cutoffs are likely to cause artefacts in map calculation.

span.label: the AIMLESS scaling program, and evidence that CC1/2 is a better resolution criterion than the traditional <I/sigma> - together with the finding that extending past the conventional limit `does no harm`
span.quote: The effective ‘resolution’ of a data set is a difficult and possibly contentious question (particularly with referees of papers) and this is discussed in the light of tests comparing the data-processing statistics with trials of refinement against observed and simulated data, and automated model-building and comparison of maps calculated with different resolution limits. These trials show that adding weak high-resolution data beyond the commonly used limits may make some improvement and does no harm.

span.label: method
span.quote: A better measure for assessing the ‘resolution’ of a data set is the correlation coefficient between random half data sets, CC 1/2 (labelled ‘CC_Imean’ in older versions of SCALA ; Evans, 2006 ▶ , 2011 ▶ ; Karplus & Diederichs, 2012 ▶ ). This statistic is plotted against resolution in both SCALA and AIMLESS (Fig. 2 ▶ ). A related statistic, Fourier shell correlation, has been used for assessing the resolution of electron-microscopy reconstructions since the early 1980s (see, for example, Rosenthal & Henderson, 2003 ▶ ; Henderson et al. , 2012 ▶ ). The advantage of a correlation coefficient is that it has a well defined range: +1.0 for a good correlation and 0 for no correlation. CC 1/2 is generally close to 1 at low resolution and falls sharply to near zero at higher resolution as the intensities become weaker

span.label: a threshold whose value depends on the use the data is put to, and whose main friction is with referees
span.quote: A major cause of user indecision and conflicts with journal referees is the resolution cutoff. We cannot set definite rules for this, as it depends on what the data are to be used for. It is therefore a mistake to prematurely apply a harsh cutoff at the data-reduction stage: data can always be excluded later. It is also unclear how best to handle anisotropy: do you choose the best direction or the worst? It is probably best to include data to the limit in the best direction.

span.label: refinement against measured and simulated data at a range of cutoffs, automated model building at four resolutions, and OMIT-map comparison - with the data-processing statistics recorded at each point
span.term: refinement against measured and simulated data at a range of cutoffs, automated model building at four resolutions, and OMIT-map comparison - with the data-processing statistics recorded at each point
span.quote: Similar tests were carried out for examples 4 and 5 (see Figs. 2 ▶ e and 2 ▶ f ), with similar conclusions that by the time CC 1/2 has fallen to around 0.2–0.4, or 〈 I /σ〉 to around 0.5–1.5, there is little information remaining, but that it would be hard to make a definite rule. With increasing resolution the R factors and D values for experimental data converge towards the values from simulated data, but the point at which they coalesce relative to the data-processing scores varies between different scores and different data sets.

span.label: **A THRESHOLD PAPER THAT REFUSES TO SET THE THRESHOLD, AND SAYS WHY**: `A MAJOR CAUSE OF USER INDECISION AND CONFLICTS WITH JOURNAL REFEREES IS THE RESOLUTION CUTOFF. WE CANNOT SET DEFINITE RULES FOR THIS, AS IT DEPENDS ON WHAT THE DATA ARE TO BE USED FOR. It is therefore A MISTAKE TO PREMATURELY APPLY A HARSH CUTOFF at the data-reduction stage: DATA CAN ALWAYS BE EXCLUDED LATER.` Three things at once - the friction is social, the value is purpose-dependent, and the advice is about WHEN to apply a criterion rather than where to put it
span.quote: A major cause of user indecision and conflicts with journal referees is the resolution cutoff. We cannot set definite rules for this, as it depends on what the data are to be used for. It is therefore a mistake to prematurely apply a harsh cutoff at the data-reduction stage: data can always be excluded later. It is also unclear how best to handle anisotropy: do you choose the best direction or the worst? It is probably best to include data to the limit in the best direction.

span.label: AND THE CONVENTION AND THE MEASUREMENT DISAGREE, IN ANGSTROMS: `there is NO GAIN in including data beyond about 1.95 A resolution, at which point CC1/2 IS 0.27 and <I/sigma> IS 0.9: A MORE CONVENTIONAL CUTOFF POINT AT <I/sigma> = 2.0 WOULD BE AT 2.06 A RESOLUTION.` The traditional criterion throws away a shell of data the tests say is still useful - and the gap is 0.11 A on one data set
span.quote: We could conclude from this that there is no gain in including data beyond about 1.95 Å resolution, at which point CC 1/2 is 0.27 and 〈 I /σ〉 is 0.9: a more conventional cutoff point at 〈 I /σ〉 = 2.0 would be at 2.06 Å resolution. This data set is significantly anisotropic, with orthogonal principal axes along d1 = 0.97 h + 0.23 l , d2 = k , d3 = −0.75 h + 0.67 l , with the resolutions at which 〈 I /σ〉 = 2.0 along d1 , d2 and d3 being 2.23, 1.98 and 2.05

span.label: **AND THE THRESHOLD IS NOT A SCALAR**: the same data set gives `the resolutions at which <I/sigma> = 2.0 along d1, d2 and d3 being 2.23, 1.98 AND 2.05 A` - three answers depending on direction. And the paper declines to choose: `it is NOT CLEAR whether it is better to include data based on THE BEST DIRECTION, THE WORST, OR SOMETHING IN BETWEEN. ANISOTROPIC CUTOFFS ARE LIKELY TO CAUSE ARTEFACTS in map calculation`
span.quote: How can we decide where to apply a resolution cutoff? On the one hand, using high-resolution data which are so weak as to be insignificant will add nothing useful, may add unwanted noise to maps and may lead us to overconfidence in the quality of our model (although the relationship between data quality and model quality is not clear). On the other hand, we do not want to exclude useful data which might aid structure solution and improve the final model. Anisotropy in the data complicates this decision, as it is not clear whether it is better to include data based on the best direction, the worst, or something in between. Anisotropic cutoffs are likely to cause artefacts in map calculation.

span.label: AND THE EMPIRICAL RANGE IS GIVEN AND THEN REFUSED AS A RULE: `by the time CC1/2 HAS FALLEN TO AROUND 0.2-0.4, or <I/sigma> TO AROUND 0.5-1.5, there is little information remaining, BUT THAT IT WOULD BE HARD TO MAKE A DEFINITE RULE. ... THE POINT AT WHICH THEY COALESCE relative to the data-processing scores VARIES BETWEEN DIFFERENT SCORES AND DIFFERENT DATA SETS.` A range published as a range, with the reason it cannot become a number
span.quote: Similar tests were carried out for examples 4 and 5 (see Figs. 2 ▶ e and 2 ▶ f ), with similar conclusions that by the time CC 1/2 has fallen to around 0.2–0.4, or 〈 I /σ〉 to around 0.5–1.5, there is little information remaining, but that it would be hard to make a definite rule. With increasing resolution the R factors and D values for experimental data converge towards the values from simulated data, but the point at which they coalesce relative to the data-processing scores varies between different scores and different data sets.

span.label: **AND A QUALITY STATISTIC THAT GETS WORSE AS THE DATA GETS BETTER**: `The multiplicity-weighted R_meas is an improvement over R_merge, as it is RELATIVELY INSENSITIVE TO DATA MULTIPLICITY, WHEREAS R_MERGE TENDS TO INCREASE WITH INCREASING MULTIPLICITY, EVEN THOUGH THE AVERAGED INTENSITIES ARE IMPROVING.` The measure and the thing measured move in opposite directions, and the field used the bad one for decades
span.quote: Internal consistency has traditionally been measured by R factors relating an individual observation I h l (after scaling) to the (weighted) average of all symmetry-related or replicate observations of the unique reflection h , 〈 I h 〉. The multiplicity-weighted R meas is an improvement over R merge , as it is relatively insensitive to data multiplicity (Diederichs & Karplus, 1997 ▶ ; Weiss & Hilgenfeld, 1997 ▶ ; Weiss, 2001 ▶ ), whereas R merge tends to increase with increasing multiplicity, even though the averaged intensities are improving. R p.i.m. provides an estimate of data quality after merging multiple observations. An alternative way of measuring internal consistency for the analysis against resolution is to split the observations randomly into halves and then calculate the linear correlation coefficient between the halves. This is arguably the most reliable measure and is discussed further below.

span.label: AND THE CONSISTENCY MEASURE CANNOT SEE THE ERROR THAT MATTERS MOST: `Note that INTERNAL CONSISTENCY MEASURES ARE LIKELY TO UNDERESTIMATE THE TRUE ERROR, SINCE SYMMETRY-RELATED OBSERVATIONS MAY SUFFER FROM THE SAME SYSTEMATIC ERROR.` Agreement between replicates is evidence of precision and silent about accuracy - the measurement's blind spot is exactly the error class it is used to rule out
span.quote: Once we have a set of scale factors to put all the intensities on a common scale and improved estimates of the error on each intensity, then we can analyse the data for internal consistency and for signal-to-noise ratio. We can do this as a function of image number (equivalent to time or crystal rotation) to detect radiation damage and weak or inconsistent regions of data and against resolution to decide on a high-resolution cutoff (see §4 ). Note that internal consistency measures are likely to underestimate the true error, since symmetry-related observations may suffer from the same systematic error.

span.label: AND THE ERROR BARS ARE WRONG EVERYWHERE, BY DEFAULT: `Initial estimates of the standard error of each intensity observation ARE GENERALLY UNDERESTIMATED BY ALL INTEGRATION PROGRAMS, so AIMLESS ... UPDATES THE sigma(I) ESTIMATES in an attempt to make the average standard error match the average scatter.` Every program in the field ships an underestimate, and the fix is a fitted correction
span.quote: Initial estimates of the standard error of each intensity observation, σ( I h l ), are generally underestimated by all integration programs, so AIMLESS , like SCALA , updates the σ( I ) estimates in an attempt to make the average standard error match the average scatter of observations as a function of intensity only. The mismatch arises partly from the unknown ‘gain’ of the detector ( i.e. detector units per photon), which scales the Poisson-statistic error estimates (as well as correcting for the detector point-spread function), and partly from a variety of instrumental instabilities which cause an increase in error with increasing intensity.

span.label: AND ONE OF THE CORRECTION TERMS HAS NO MEANING: `SdB HAS NO OBVIOUS PHYSICAL INTERPRETATION. However, this factor HELPS TO FLATTEN THE PLOT of variance against intensity and MAY BE JUSTIFIED AS AN EMPIRICAL `CORRECTION` FACTOR. It should be noted that this `correction` to the error estimates is A FAIRLY CRUDE APPROXIMATION, as it ASSUMES THERE ARE NO MAJOR RESIDUAL SYSTEMATIC ERRORS.` A parameter kept because it works, labelled as such, with the assumption it rests on printed beside it
span.quote: Sdfac can be identified primarily with the uncertainty in the detector gain and Sdadd with general instability factors which lead to an error proportional to intensity (see, for example, Diederichs, 2010 ▶ ), but SbB has no obvious physical interpretation. However, this factor helps to flatten the plot of variance(δ h l ) against intensity and may be justified as an empirical ‘correction’ factor. It should be noted that this ‘correction’ to the error estimates is a fairly crude approximation, as it assumes there are no major residual systematic errors (such as those arising from radiation damage, for example) and that the correction can be parameterized purely on intensity.

span.label: AND THE PREFERRED STATISTIC WAS BORROWED FROM ANOTHER FIELD THIRTY YEARS EARLIER: `A BETTER MEASURE for assessing the `resolution` of a data set is THE CORRELATION COEFFICIENT BETWEEN RANDOM HALF DATA SETS, CC1/2 ... A RELATED STATISTIC, FOURIER SHELL CORRELATION, HAS BEEN USED FOR ASSESSING THE RESOLUTION OF ELECTRON-MICROSCOPY RECONSTRUCTIONS SINCE THE EARLY 1980s.` The advantage given is definitional: `a correlation coefficient ... HAS A WELL DEFINED RANGE`
span.quote: A better measure for assessing the ‘resolution’ of a data set is the correlation coefficient between random half data sets, CC 1/2 (labelled ‘CC_Imean’ in older versions of SCALA ; Evans, 2006 ▶ , 2011 ▶ ; Karplus & Diederichs, 2012 ▶ ). This statistic is plotted against resolution in both SCALA and AIMLESS (Fig. 2 ▶ ). A related statistic, Fourier shell correlation, has been used for assessing the resolution of electron-microscopy reconstructions since the early 1980s (see, for example, Rosenthal & Henderson, 2003 ▶ ; Henderson et al. , 2012 ▶ ). The advantage of a correlation coefficient is that it has a well defined range: +1.0 for a good correlation and 0 for no correlation. CC 1/2 is generally close to 1 at low resolution and falls sharply to near zero at higher resolution as the intensities become weaker

span.label: THE MODEL-BUILDING TEST COULD NOT SEPARATE ANYTHING: `There have been ANECDOTAL REPORTS that extending the resolution to include weak data may help automated model-building procedures. UNFORTUNATELY, THIS HAS BEEN HARD TO PROVE: THE EXAMPLES TRIED HERE EITHER WORKED AT ALL RESOLUTIONS OR LARGELY FAILED AT ALL RESOLUTIONS ... there was NO CONSISTENT PATTERN over the different resolutions.` A negative result reported as a negative result, on the question the whole paper is about
span.quote: There have been anecdotal reports that extending the resolution to include weak data may help automated model-building procedures. Unfortunately, this has been hard to prove: the examples tried here either worked at all resolutions or largely failed at all resolutions. Example 2 was used to test model building from a rather poor map with experimental phases to 2.5 Å resolution and model building with the Buccaneer / REFMAC pipeline (Cowtan, 2012 ▶ ) tested at resolutions of 2.3, 2.4, 2.5 and 2.6 Å. Models built at all of these resolutions had some correct and some incorrect parts, with the assigned sequence being largely wrong, but there was no consistent pattern over the different resolutions in the number of residues built or sequence assignment or in the correctness of the models.

span.label: AND MERGING MORE DATA CAN MAKE IT WORSE: `merging many data sets USUALLY IMPROVES the signal-to-noise ratio in the data; HOWEVER, IT IS NOT CLEAR HOW TO MERGE DATA WHEN THERE IS SEVERE NON-ISOMORPHISM OR RADIATION DAMAGE.` More observations is not always more information, and the paper says where the boundary is unknown rather than guessing at it
span.quote: At the end, model quality depends on data quality and merging many data sets usually improves the signal-to-noise ratio in the data; however, it is not clear how to merge data when there is severe non-isomorphism or radiation damage.

span.label: and the relationship the cutoff is supposed to serve is itself unclear: `using high-resolution data which are so weak as to be insignificant will ADD NOTHING USEFUL, may add unwanted noise to maps and MAY LEAD US TO OVERCONFIDENCE IN THE QUALITY OF OUR MODEL (ALTHOUGH THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN DATA QUALITY AND MODEL QUALITY IS NOT CLEAR).` The parenthesis undercuts the sentence it is inside, and the authors leave it there
span.quote: How can we decide where to apply a resolution cutoff? On the one hand, using high-resolution data which are so weak as to be insignificant will add nothing useful, may add unwanted noise to maps and may lead us to overconfidence in the quality of our model (although the relationship between data quality and model quality is not clear). Anisotropic cutoffs are likely to cause artefacts in map calculation.

span.label: refining against SIMULATED data generated from the observed intensity distribution but NOT from the structure itself, at the same resolutions as the measured data

span.label: R meas
span.quote: Internal consistency has traditionally been measured by R factors relating an individual observation I h l (after scaling) to the (weighted) average of all symmetry-related or replicate observations of the unique reflection h , 〈 I h 〉. The multiplicity-weighted R meas is an improvement over R merge , as it is relatively insensitive to data multiplicity (Diederichs & Karplus, 1997 ▶ ; Weiss & Hilgenfeld, 1997 ▶ ; Weiss, 2001 ▶ ), whereas R merge tends to increase with increasing multiplicity, even though the averaged intensities are improving. R p.i.m. provides an estimate of data quality after merging multiple observations. An alternative way of measuring internal consistency for the analysis against resolution is to split the observations randomly into halves and then calculate the linear correlation coefficient between the halves. This is arguably the most reliable measure and is discussed further below.

span.quote: A major cause of user indecision and conflicts with journal referees is the resolution cutoff. We cannot set definite rules for this, as it depends on what the data are to be used for. It is also unclear how best to handle anisotropy: do you choose the best direction or the worst? It is probably best to include data to the limit in the best direction.

span.quote: Internal consistency has traditionally been measured by R factors relating an individual observation I h l (after scaling) to the (weighted) average of all symmetry-related or replicate observations of the unique reflection h , 〈 I h 〉. The multiplicity-weighted R meas is an improvement over R merge , as it is relatively insensitive to data multiplicity (Diederichs & Karplus, 1997 ▶ ; Weiss & Hilgenfeld, 1997 ▶ ; Weiss, 2001 ▶ ), whereas R merge tends to increase with increasing multiplicity, even though the averaged intensities are improving. R p.i.m. provides an estimate of data quality after merging multiple observations. An alternative way of measuring internal consistency for the analysis against resolution is to split the observations randomly into halves and then calculate the linear correlation coefficient between the halves. This is arguably the most reliable measure and is discussed further below.

span.quote: Once we have a set of scale factors to put all the intensities on a common scale and improved estimates of the error on each intensity, then we can analyse the data for internal consistency and for signal-to-noise ratio. We can do this as a function of image number (equivalent to time or crystal rotation) to detect radiation damage and weak or inconsistent regions of data and against resolution to decide on a high-resolution cutoff (see §4 ). Note that internal consistency measures are likely to underestimate the true error, since symmetry-related observations may suffer from the same systematic error.

However, this factor helps to flatten the plot of variance(δ h l ) against intensity and may be justified as an empirical ‘correction’ factor. It should be noted that this ‘correction’ to the error estimates is a fairly crude approximation, as it assumes there are no major residual systematic errors (such as those arising from radiation damage, for example) and that the correction can be parameterized purely on intensity.

span.quote: A better measure for assessing the ‘resolution’ of a data set is the correlation coefficient between random half data sets, CC 1/2 (labelled ‘CC_Imean’ in older versions of SCALA ; Evans, 2006 ▶ , 2011 ▶ ; Karplus & Diederichs, 2012 ▶ ). This statistic is plotted against resolution in both SCALA and AIMLESS (Fig. 2 ▶ ). A related statistic, Fourier shell correlation, has been used for assessing the resolution of electron-microscopy reconstructions since the early 1980s (see, for example, Rosenthal & Henderson, 2003 ▶ ; Henderson et al. , 2012 ▶ ). The advantage of a correlation coefficient is that it has a well defined range: +1.0 for a good correlation and 0 for no correlation. CC 1/2 is generally close to 1 at low resolution and falls sharply to near zero at higher resolution as the intensities become weaker

span.label: `A DIFFICULT AND POSSIBLY CONTENTIOUS QUESTION (PARTICULARLY WITH REFEREES OF PAPERS)` - and `WE CANNOT SET DEFINITE RULES FOR THIS, AS IT DEPENDS ON WHAT THE DATA ARE TO BE USED FOR`
span.quote: The effective ‘resolution’ of a data set is a difficult and possibly contentious question (particularly with referees of papers) and this is discussed in the light of tests comparing the data-processing statistics with trials of refinement against observed and simulated data, and automated model-building and comparison of maps calculated with different resolution limits. These trials show that adding weak high-resolution data beyond the commonly used limits may make some improvement and does no harm.

span.label: the per-observation sigma the signal-to-noise criterion divides by - and it is `GENERALLY UNDERESTIMATED BY ALL INTEGRATION PROGRAMS`, so the traditional cutoff of I/sigma = 2.0 is a threshold on a quantity every program gets wrong by default
span.quote: Initial estimates of the standard error of each intensity observation, σ( I h l ), are generally underestimated by all integration programs, so AIMLESS , like SCALA , updates the σ( I ) estimates in an attempt to make the average standard error match the average scatter of observations as a function of intensity only. The mismatch arises partly from the unknown ‘gain’ of the detector ( i.e. detector units per photon), which scales the Poisson-statistic error estimates (as well as correcting for the detector point-spread function), and partly from a variety of instrumental instabilities which cause an increase in error with increasing intensity.
